name: TomsFastMath
listed_description: Set of optimized maths operations (in assembly)
reason: No numeric comparison against a named baseline on any page reachable. The github.com README, doc/tfm.tex and demo/timing.c have no numbers against any other library (timing.c only times TFM itself). The libtom.net page, which a search snippet says claims 'faster than OpenSSL on the AMD64', was EGRESS_BLOCKED and the snippet gives no numbers. A Dropbear mailing-list thread ('slow logins -- some data for comparison', 2013, lists.ucc.gu.uwa.edu.au) reportedly shows login time falling from about 45 s to 30 s when switching from LibTomMath to TomsFastMath on a slow Microblaze system, but that page was EGRESS_BLOCKED (snippet only, baseline LibTomMath, not OpenSSL BN). The libzahl STATUS file (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/maandree/libzahl/HEAD/STATUS) lists TomsFastMath as faster than libzahl and GMP on a few small-operand functions (zseti, zsetu, zand, zor, zdiv) without numbers for TomsFastMath itself, and notes that its compile-time size limit gives it a significant performance advantage. Last release 0.13.1 (2017).

name: tungsten
listed_description: A high-performance physically based renderer in C++.
reason: Not a numerics library: it is a physically based path/photon-mapping renderer (zlib licence, 1.8k stars) built on Embree. The README only says it 'tries to offer good performance through frequent benchmarking and optimization' and gives no numbers or comparison against Mitsuba, pbrt, Cycles or any physics engine; the guessed baseline (ODE or Bullet Physics) and category (blas-lapack) do not apply. A search for render-time comparisons found none (only an OpenBenchmarking test profile that runs Tungsten alone).

name: universal
listed_description: A C++14 header-only library implementing arbitrary posit arithmetic. The posit number system is a tapered floating point that is more efficient than IEEE floating point. Posits enable reproducible computational science.
reason: No speed claim against a named baseline. The README states only general benefits of tailored number systems (speed-ups of two to three orders of magnitude for deep learning formats such as half precision and bfloat16, not measured on this library) and a 20% AVX2 build-flag gain; benchmark/README.md just links openbenchmarking.org and the repo has no published comparison with MPFR, GMP, Boost.Multiprecision or SoftFloat. Search snippets of the project's own paper (arXiv 2012.11011) say its software posits and reference implementation are slower than hardware IEEE float, SoftFloat and MPFR. It is a collection of number systems (posit, fixed-point, cascade/multi-component floats, arbitrary integers), not a big-integer library; the guessed category does not fit.
